The best chain is QB11-QB12-QB7, with QB12 in the middle. I took it from Garnet's current default calibration (set 9069c4ef-7ab6-4e50-be4f-c91d71c3a06d). I checked all 30 CZ pairs on Garnet and every chain of 3 qubits they form.

- The CZ fidelity of QB11-QB12 is 0.99945.
- The CZ fidelity of QB12-QB7 is 0.99907.
- Their product is 0.99852. That is the highest of any chain.
- The next best chain is QB11-QB12-QB17, with a product of 0.99818.

I then ran a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly QB11, QB12 and QB7 on garnet:mock with 200 shots. The job ID is 01a16482-37e5-7146-8c61-fd307117bdd2 and it completed. The circuit puts QB12 into an equal mix of 0 and 1 with a single-qubit rotation. Then two CZ gates, one on QB12-QB11 and one on QB12-QB7, link the outer qubits to QB12. A final rotation on each outer qubit turns that link into "copy the middle bit". All 3 qubits are measured. I read the job back from the server to confirm it. The server received exactly 2 CZ gates, on QB12-QB11 and QB12-QB7, and it measured QB11, QB12 and QB7.

The counts are in the order QB11, QB12, QB7:
- 000: 52
- 011: 47
- 100: 51
- 111: 50

A perfect quantum computer would give 000 half the time and 111 half the time, and nothing else. I simulated the exact circuit without noise, and it gave that result. The GHZ state shows entanglement. Each qubit on its own is a random coin flip, but all 3 always agree. The mock counts do not show this because the mock returns random results that ignore the circuit. So these counts test only that the job ran. They are not physics data. On the real Garnet you would expect mostly 000 and 111, with a few other results caused by gate and readout errors. The mock run cost 0 credits, even though the API reports 1.0 billed second for it.
